BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: As the closed upper low continues to steer eastward across our area and the Great Basin, continuous valley rain and mountain snow showers will be expected through most of Thursday as the precipitation tapers off over southwest ID late Thursday through early Friday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Valley rain and mountain snow over southeast Oregon will expand into southwest Idaho tonight.
- Cool and wet pattern with valley rain and mountain snow through Tuesday and returning late Wednesday through Friday.
- Possible return of another cool and wet pattern late Saturday through early next week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: The slow-moving cold front will continue to trek eastward across our area this morning through Tuesday. Widespread valley rain and mountain snow will continue over the area today, with the continuous rain band currently over eastern OR and the ID/OR border expected to steer into southwest ID by tonight. Snow levels will hover in the 6500-7500 ft range through most of today, favoring rain over most areas and light snowfall over high mountain peaks. Precipitation will taper off over southwest ID Tuesday morning, as the front moves out of our area by Tuesday afternoon. The cold frontal passage will begin a gradual cooling trend from today through the end of the short term period, with temperatures lowering down to near or slightly below normal through midweek. Snow levels will drop into the 3500-4500 ft range by early Tuesday. Late Tuesday through early Wednesday, a brief ridge of high pressure will build over the area, bringing a dry break from Tuesday afternoon through Wednesday morning. This break will be short-lived, as a deep Pacific upper low sweeps into the northwest and Great Basin on Wednesday, returning a swath of eastward moving precipitation throughout the area. With snow levels expected to drop to valley floors by early Wednesday, widespread snow showers are expected across eastern OR, with accumulations up to 1 inch possible by late Wednesday. The lower Treasure Valley can see rain/snow mixes or dusting of snow in the morning hours of Wednesday, before snow levels climb back up to the 3500-4500 ft range by the afternoon. The rest of Wednesday will see widespread valley rain and mountain snow.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: As the closed upper low continues to steer eastward across our area and the Great Basin, continuous valley rain and mountain snow showers will be expected through most of Thursday as the precipitation tapers off over southwest ID late Thursday through early Friday. Lower valley areas are tentatively looking at around 0.20 inches of total rainfall by early Friday. Latest long-range guidance has snow levels hanging in the 3500-4500 ft range through Saturday. Valleys can see a rain/snow mix Friday morning, before precipitation completely tapers off by late Friday. Mountain peaks can still see possible total snow accumulations of 5 to 10 inches by early Saturday. Temperatures are expected to hover near or slightly below normal Thursday through the weekend. Come early Saturday, the system will steer out of our area as a ridge builds in behind it. This brief dry period will be limited, as the latest long-term guidance now has another Pacific upper trough moving into the northwest and into the eastern OR side by late Saturday. Come Sunday, there is uncertainty over whether the trough will bring a highly moist shortwave and return widespread precipitation or steer north of our area and bring limited precipitation. For now, slight to moderate chances of valley rain or rain/snow mix and mountain snow showers are forecasted for late Saturday through early Monday, with higher terrain areas seeing the bulk of total precip.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: There should be a brief break between systems on Thursday, with mild and generally quiet weather across the state. The next system arrives Friday and looks a little more organized and longer lasting, as a broad trough axis moves through the region.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Remaining mild and dry across the plains over the next several days.
- Chances for mountain snow late Tuesday night into Wednesday morning, and again Friday into Saturday.
- Gusty winds possible across the Front Range mountains and foothills Tuesday night into Wednesday.

sections.name: Update
paragraphs: Webcams show fog has become dense in areas along I-76 fromBrighton to Sterling. Because of this, decided to issue a Dense Fog Advisory until 10 AM.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: A mix of stratus, mist, and fog are evident across the eastern plains tonight. Based on surface observations, most of the lower visibilities seem to be east of the main stratus deck that has persisted across Lincoln county into the far northeastern corner this evening. Short term guidance continues to develop additional fog across most of the Platte River valley into the northern/northwestern Denver metro, though recent HRRR runs have backed off of the southwestern extent of this fog through Monday AM. We've kept patchy fog in the grids across most of the lower elevations but did trim some of it out of the I-25 corridor.

Monday should be a mild day across most of our forecast area as the ridge axis shifts eastward. We'll have broad but dry southwesterly flow aloft during the day ahead of our next shortwave, with temperatures again reaching the low to mid 60s across the plains. Similar conditions are expected on Tuesday as the shortwave continues to approach the region and the mid-level flow strengthens in response. Highs are likely to reach the mid 60s in the metro with some guidance hinting at potentially warmer temperatures.

The first of two storm systems will reach the area on Wednesday, though this one looks to only provide a glancing blow to the region as it quickly ejects into the northern Rockies/northern Great Plains. Guidance does have a decent push of moisture across the western half of the state Tuesday night, but quickly dries us out as the mid-level low pushes into northeastern Montana during the day Wednesday. While the 700-500mb flow briefly is favorable for orographic snow showers, the limited duration of sufficient moisture will keep snow accumulations to a minimum (generally an inch or less). The main story this period may be wind, as this looks to be our first bora type event of the season. Cross sections reveal a brief/marginally favorable mountain wave amplification setup Wednesday morning. I am a bit skeptical of the higher end solution advertised by the RRFS at this time, but 50kt cross barrier flow along with a modest stable layer would support a few gusts near high wind criteria over the Front Range mountains and higher foothills. On the other hand, any additional northward shift with this shortwave would likely limit wind potential across our forecast area.

There should be a brief break between systems on Thursday, with mild and generally quiet weather across the state. The next system arrives Friday and looks a little more organized and longer lasting, as a broad trough axis moves through the region. While this is still unlikely to produce much (other than maybe some gusty winds) across the plains, the overall setup does look more favorable for mountain snow across the northern half of the state. Guidance generally features a longer period of orographic snow, initially supported by some QG ascent and a favorable jet position. Chances for snow should linger into Saturday before moisture diminishes on Sunday.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Seasonal temperatures will stick around on Thursday with little to no weather impacts expected. Some lingering breezy conditions are still possible on Thursday, but overall, will be a quiet day.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Patchy fog will again be possible into Monday morning, mainly for locations in the far eastern Nebraska Panhandle.

- A High Wind Watch is now in effect for the Wind Prone areas of southeast Wyoming and some of the adjacent sub-wind prone areas along highway 287 and Interstate 25 north of Wheatland. Gusts over 65+ MPH are possible late Tuesday night through Wednesday evening.
- A chance for a few rain and snow showers Tuesday night into Wednesday, mainly across portions of Carbon and Albany Counties. Another chance for rain and snow possible late Friday into Saturday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Current observations and 10.3-3.9 um IR loop shows a much lower coverage of low clouds and fog early this morning compared to the last several days with a few patches near Pine Bluffs and south of Kimball. Other than some development further north near Scottsbluff, not expect this fog to become a big deal this morning with it likely lifting around sunrise. At most, will likely handle lower visibility with a Special Weather Statement due to limited areal coverage. Otherwise, models show even warmer temperatures for today as a Pacific shortwave ridge axis translates eastward into the Intermountain West and amplifies over the Front Range. Pleasant mid-November day expected with highs in the upper 50s to mid 60s.

All models show the next Pacific storm system rapidly moving onshore, producing rainfall as far south as southern Calif and mountain/Great Basin snowfall late Monday and Tuesday. This will be our next weather maker which is forecast to impact the region late Tuesday night and Wednesday. As of right now, models are not indicating a closed storm system and still show an open wave trough ejecting northeast over Wyoming and Montana. This storm track favors mountains snow, cooler temperatures, and windy conditions across southeast Wyoming. In-house wind guidance have remained consistent with high probabilities (70%+) of strong gusty winds for the wind prone areas and some of the sub wind prone areas through Wednesday. With an excellent mountain wave signature depicted on high res models and all synoptic models showing 700mb winds between 60 to 70 knots through noon Wednesday with ample downward Omega, decided to issue a High Wind Watch for all wind prone areas, northern Carbon County near Muddy Gap, and eastern Platte County which is a favorable sub wind prone region for mountain wave enhanced gusts. Converse County, the Laramie Valley, central Carbon County, and the Cheyenne area may also see strong gusty winds, but confidence is not as high for these areas compared to the zones listed above. High Wind Watch will be valid until 10 PM late Wednesday evening.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: A pattern change will arrive on Wednesday as a trough swings into the Rockies. A cold front will move across the area, late Tuesday night or early Wednesday morning, leading to high temperatures in the 40s and 50s--roughly average for this time of year. This front will be mostly dry, with predominately west winds promoting a dry downslope environment. The mountains, however, could see a quick shot of snow, with the Sierra Madre Range picking up a few inches of accumulation. The Snowys will likely be shadowed and not see much in the way of accumulations. The bigger concern with the frontal passage will be strong winds. More recent model runs show a strong potential for high winds. MSLP gradients will compress from the front as well as CAG to CPR 850 and 700 mb heights. Height values are rather impressive, with 850 mb heights reaching over 70 meters and 700 mb heights well over 60 meters. These values are typically indicative of strong high winds around the Arlington area. Winds aloft also look much stronger compared to previous runs of the GFS. 750 mb winds max out at over 70 kts over the Laramie Range by mid- day with very strong subsidence. Subsidence alone will likely be enough to allow these winds to reach the surface at Bordeaux and the South Laramie Range and foothills. Could even see high winds in the wind prone adjacent areas along Interstate 25 as cross sections of omega and potential temperature show a strong mountain wave signature. Winds gusts between 60 and 70 MPH will be likely, especially in the wind prones, with stronger gusts possible if this trend holds. Winds will weaken by Wednesday evening as the trough moves out of the CWA.

Seasonal temperatures will stick around on Thursday with little to no weather impacts expected. Some lingering breezy conditions are still possible on Thursday, but overall, will be a quiet day. Friday into the weekend, things could get interesting with a potential winter storm. Global models continue to trend QPF/snowfall totals down across the forecast area as the trough becomes more of a progressive open wave instead of a closed off low. Many ensemble members of both the GFS and the ECMWF don't even show any QPF for areas east of the Laramie Range, a far cry from the runs of a few days ago showing a major winter storm. Of course, its still over a week away, so models could change, but what is more certain is that it will likely be cooler and windier during this time period.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: Forecast models continue to show another system arriving late Thursday night through Saturday morning. Models still show an open wave setup.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Dry and mild conditions Monday with morning fog possible.
- The next system will bring valley rain and mountain snow on Tuesday and Wednesday, followed closely by another storm system on Friday and Saturday.
- Mountain passes could see adverse travel conditions Tuesday night and Wednesday morning.
- Temperatures will trend downward late week, with colder air delivering the first freezing temperatures for some desert valleys.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Skies across the region are mostly clear with some thin high clouds working eastward. Some thicker cloud cover has pushed into northeast UT ahead of the trough moving ashore on the West Coast tonight. Cloud cover will be notable early Monday morning, as it could hinder some of the fog and low stratus we saw develop on Sunday morning. Satellite imagery at this hour shows a little bit of stratus developing in southwest CO. The abundant surface moisture down there will encourage fog, should we radiate out properly overnight. Dewpoint depressions around Durango, Cortez, and Pagosa Springs are already near zero.

Another warm and mild day will start the work week, with temperatures around 5 degrees above average. Light winds and sunshine stick around Monday. Thin high clouds begin to invade the region ahead of Tuesday's storm. This will usher in a series of pattern shifts across the region. Strong southwesterly winds develop Tuesday on the backside of the departing high pressure. This will push temperatures up nearly 10 degrees above normal and bring moisture back into the region along a weak frontal boundary. These warm temperatures will keep snow levels in the 9-10k range for our mountain groups, with rain in the valleys below Tuesday afternoon and early Wednesday morning. Snow totals have ebbed some on this latest model run. Winter headlines could come into play across the San Juans on Tuesday night. Gusty winds beneath a potent jet streak could stir up a lot of blowing snow on Tuesday evening. Travelers will want to stay abreast of local conditions on mountain roads, as visibility and road conditions could deteriorate rather quickly in the evening hours as the frontal boundary works across the region.

Snow will taper pretty quickly around daybreak Wednesday, as this system crosses the Divide. A few lingering snow showers will continue along the Divide Wednesday morning. Commuters on the passes are likely to see some slick roads too. Cooler and drier conditions develop on Wednesday with temperatures 10 to 15 degrees colder behind the front. A weak transitory ridge moves overhead Wednesday and Thursday as another more organized system comes ashore out west.

Forecast models continue to show another system arriving late Thursday night through Saturday morning. Models still show an open wave setup. Precipitation totals continue to vary by model run, with the central and northern mountains of Colorado picking up additional snow in the latest runs. Differences among the models with regards to strength and timing keep confidence low attm. Most of the moisture is expected to arrive ahead of the cold front, making timing critical. Snow levels could drop to some valley floors Friday night into Saturday morning. For now, however, the specifics remain uncertain.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Dry and mild on Thu, then the next windy upper trough moves through the area Thu night into Fri night.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Low clouds and patchy fog across the plains this morning, clearing this afternoon, then dry and warmer on Tuesday.
- Quick-moving system to bring snow to the Continental Divide Tuesday evening through Wednesday morning, with gusty winds area-wide.
- Another slightly stronger system to bring mountain snow and wind Thursday night through Friday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Upper ridge moves over the Rockies today, as old upper low shifts eastward into the lower Mississippi Valley. Low clouds and patchy fog will linger on the plains this morning before enough mixing develops to dissipate things by midday. More sun and better mixing will give high temps a boost, with readings in the mountains 2-5 degf warmer than yesterday, while the plains rise 5-10 degf. Drier boundary layer should then preclude a return of stratus/fog tonight, with temps falling into the 20s/30s across the region

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Breezy and warmer weather expected on Tuesday, as next western U.S. upper trough moves into the Great Basin by afternoon. Plains will see readings deep into the 60s Tue, with a couple near 70 degf readings in the lower Arkansas Valley. A few showers will reach the San Juans toward sunset, though daytime precip amounts will be light. Trough moves quickly through Colorado Tuesday night, then lifts rapidly into the nrn plain by Wed afternoon. Pattern produces only a brief window of upward motion Tue night, with the best moisture/lift favoring the eastern San Juans. Could see around 6 inches of snow at Wolf Creek Pass before snow tapers off quickly Wed morning, with only a couple inches over the central mountains and higher peaks of the Sangres. Remaining high terrain and valleys will see a few quick moving showers Tue night, with more wind (gusts 45-55 mph) than rain/snow at most locations. I-25/plains will miss precip entirely, with just a period of strong winds (gusts 35-45 mph) overnight into Wed morning. Winds then diminish Wed afternoon as upper trough quickly departs and surface gradient weakens. Mid level cold advection will drop Wed high temps 5-10 degf from Tuesday's numbers over the mountains, while deep mixing on the plains limits the amount of cooling, with readings east of I-25 still into the 60s.

Dry and mild on Thu, then the next windy upper trough moves through the area Thu night into Fri night. Models continue with a fast/northerly trend with this system, which will again keep most of the accumulating snow limited to areas along the Continental Divide (ern San Juans favored). Remaining high terrain will see a round of windy showers on Friday, but precip looks light at this point. Trough will bring strong winds to all of the area Fri, with gusts over 60 mph possible across the mountains, and in the 40-60 mph range over most valleys and across the plains. Dry and mild weather then returns for the weekend ahead of still another upper trough moving toward the Rockies early next week.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: Our late-week storm is still on track to be colder and longer duration, impacting the region beginning early Thursday through at least Friday night.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Valley rain and mountain snow will begin this evening and continue into Wednesday morning. The heaviest snow accumulations will be across the southern mountains, where a winter weather advisory remains in effect from this evening through Tuesday evening.

- An even colder system will impacts the region Thursday into Friday, with more substantial snowfall expected for all Utah mountains. Light valley snow accumulations are increasing in likelihood by Friday afternoon near 5000 feet, to valley floors Friday night.
- Freezing temperatures are increasing in probability for lower Washington County and the Virgin River corridor near Zion National Park Saturday and Sunday morning

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Dry and mild conditions continue overnight and through a majority of Monday under increasing southwesterly flow aloft ahead of our next weather system. High-res guidance indicates showery precipitation beginning across southwest Utah as early as Monday evening, with the bulk of moisture moving in mid- to-late Tuesday morning as the associated upper-level shortwave trough pivots into the Great Basin. Expect widespread precipitation to overspread the region with this moisture surge Tuesday morning. A lull in activity is expected by early afternoon, ahead of a cold front passage late Tuesday afternoon into the evening. A quick-moving band of heavy precipitation is expected to accompany this frontal passage, with heaviest precipitation rates favored mainly across northern Utah and southwest Wyoming where dynamics will be maximized. High- res guidance indicates a more disorganized, spotty line further south into central and southern Utah late Tuesday. Shower activity will quickly dwindle behind the frontal passage, with most activity wrapped up by Tuesday night.

Snow levels will remain around 8000-9000 feet through a majority of this storm, though snow levels drop to around 5500-6000 feet behind the cold front passage late Tuesday. As such, snow accumulations are favored for Utah's mountains, particularly those above 8000 feet. Caution is advised for those traveling across high-elevation routes through this period, as accumulating snow is expected to bring dangerous travel conditions.

A brief break in active weather is expected on Wednesday as a shortwave ridge traverses the region ahead of our next storm. Of note, however, is the potential to finally reach a low of 32F or less here in SLC on Wednesday morning; current guidance indicates a 90% chance. This would be the first time SLC observes freezing temperatures this season.

Our late-week storm is still on track to be colder and longer duration, impacting the region beginning early Thursday through at least Friday night. There still remains a bit of uncertainty on how quickly the colder airmass moves into the region, however, with ensembles indicating H7 temperatures ranging between -3 to -8C Thursday afternoon. About 20% of models indicate this colder scenario that could bring snow levels close to valley floors Thursday night, while the rest indicate snow levels remaining more elevated through this period. This H7 temperature spread decreases significantly on Friday morning, with models in good agreement in temperatures around -8 to -9C, indicative of snow levels near or below valley floors. All said, this system is looking like it will bring more substantial snowfall to all Utah mountains between Thursday and Friday. The one key uncertainty at this point is if snow levels can drop quickly enough to result in measurable snow down to valley levels. Will remain something to monitor over the next few days.

2660.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Ben Pritchett
bottom_line: While you can expect generally safe avalanche concerns, monitor afternoon warming. If you find wet snow surfaces in the afternoon, consider the potential for a small loose avalanche.

2745.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Andrew McWilliams
bottom_line: Most slopes don't have enough snow for avalanches and are safe for travel. At high elevations, steer around isolated spots of firm, drifted snow below ridges or in steep gullies.

2842.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

3014.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Kevin Studley
bottom_line: Winter has yet to embrace the West Central Mountains of Idaho. Except on the steepest, highest-elevation, north-facing slopes, the mountains are snow-free. Avalanches will be unlikely until a deeper, layered snowpack builds. Once winter does arrive, even a small amount of snow with enough wind can create unstable avalanche conditions. If you're traveling in the mountains during or after a storm, be wary of steep, wind-loaded features at upper elevations and watch out for terrain traps.
We'll update the General Avalanche Information as more snow accumulates
hazard_discussion: Due to a warm and dry fall season, the mountains in our forecast zones remain mostly dry, with little to no snow on the ground. As you're waiting for winter to arrive and the mountain snowpack to stack up, here are a few things to consider:
• If you're out hiking or hunting in the mountains this fall, stay tuned to changing weather conditions. Avalanches are most likely during and immediately after a storm.

• Keep in mind the adage, "If there's enough snow to ride, there's enough snow to slide". Even if there's not enough snow to bury you, a small slide over uncovered logs, rocks, and brush would not be a fun way to start the season.
• Stay up to date on mountain weather with our WEATHER tab, where you'll find webcams, weather stations, and weather forecasting tools.

• Beacons, shovels, probes, airbags. Run through all your gear and make sure it's functioning properly. Does your transceiver or airbag need any firmware updates? Look for cracks, defects, or corroded batteries. Make it fun with your friends and do a pre-season gear check with your winter travel companions.
• Check out the Education tab on our website to sign up for avalanche courses this winter (COURSES ).
• Stay tuned to our EVENTS pages for other local happenings with winter community.
• Interested in attending a snow and avalanche workshop (SAW)? Check out A3's WEBSITE for a list of events.
• Keep an eye on our observation page HERE

• If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation HERE. Early season observations help forecasters and the public alike. A simple photo and/or weather observation helps paint the picture of where snow is and where it is not.

Yeah, that's right: the Payette Avalanche Center has a new website. Browse around before the snow starts flying. We're also on the Avy App. You can search for "Avy: Avalanche & Weather Info" in your app store on your mobile device.

2755.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Kreston Rohrig
bottom_line: Most slopes are safe for backcountry travel. If you find slightly stiffer, wind-blown drifts on a steeper slope at higher elevations, consider avoiding that terrain. There's a chance you could trigger a small avalanche.
